messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Stop Enjoyment: give up pleasant activities, Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Markus Weber is a 56-year-old combat pilot who came to treatment after months of telling himself he should be able to handle what happened. During a training flight the previous year, his aircraft suffered a catastrophic mechanical failure on descent. He remembered the first loud bang inside the cockpit, sharp and unnatural, followed by warning alarms and a violent shudder that threw his body against the harness. In the seconds before impact, he became acutely aware of his own physical sensations—lightheadedness, a sick rolling feeling in his stomach, the sense that his body was no longer reliable. He survived the crash, but the experience seemed to split his life into before and after. What stayed with him was not only the memory of the explosion-like sound and the disorientation in his body, but the conviction that the world could become lethal without warning.

In the weeks afterward, those same sensations began to feel less like ordinary bodily states and more like signals that danger was already underway. If he grew dizzy standing up too quickly, or felt vaguely unwell after a poor night’s sleep, his whole system seemed to snap tight. A slammed metal door on base or any bang resembling an explosion made him jolt before he could think. Around other people, even small unexpected movements in the room pulled a reflexive reaction out of him, as though he had to defend himself before he knew what he was seeing. He described living with his body “revved up,” constantly tense, scanning, watchful, unable to relax even at home with his wife. The dizziness and sick feeling frightened him not only because they resembled moments from the crash, but because they seemed to confirm what he had come to believe: that the world is dangerous, that the rules he trusted about skill and preparation no longer hold, and that he himself had become somehow hollowed out by the experience.

Those beliefs hardened over time. Markus had come to feel that what was destroyed in the crash was not just the aircraft, but his confidence in how life worked. He said there had always been risk in aviation, but now risk felt omnipresent, stripped of meaning or fairness. He moved through his days with a deadened quality that troubled him almost as much as the fear. He noticed that when dizziness or a sudden bang set him off, what followed was not only alarm but a bleak, immediate thought—of course this is what the world is, unsafe and ready to turn. In that state, even ordinary physical discomfort took on the force of evidence.

He began organizing his life around not setting off that chain. He avoided hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations with unusual rigidity, even when he knew routine medical care would have been sensible. He could not bear waiting rooms, the smell of antiseptic, or the suggestion that someone might check his body closely; those situations made him too aware of feeling lightheaded or ill. At work he stayed functional, but he narrowed his world outside the cockpit. He gave up dinners out, stopped meeting friends for activities he had once enjoyed, and became strict and controlling about what he ate, telling himself that if he kept his body tightly managed he might prevent the sensations that sent him spiraling. The more on guard he felt, the more he relied on these routines. If his body was going to stay primed for danger, he believed he had to compensate by controlling every variable he could.

But these efforts tightened rather than relieved things. Restricting his eating left him physically depleted at times, and the resulting lightheadedness only made the old fear more immediate. Avoiding medical settings meant he never had the chance to learn that bodily sensations could be tolerated without catastrophe, so every spell of dizziness remained potent. Pulling out of enjoyable parts of life left him more emotionally flat, and that numbness fed his sense that something vital in him had died in the crash. His wife had started commenting that he was present in the house but unreachable; Markus heard the truth in that and felt ashamed, then withdrew further. He noticed, too, that the smaller his world became, the more sharply he reacted to sounds and movement within it. A dropped tool in the hangar, a cart clattering across concrete, someone stepping unexpectedly into his peripheral vision—each seemed to prove again that he could not let his guard down.

By the time he sought help, Markus was exhausted by the discipline it took to manage each day and frightened by how little of himself he could still feel. What finally brought him in was a recent physical exam he postponed twice, then abandoned after seeing an ambulance pull up outside the clinic and feeling instantly sick and lightheaded in the parking lot. He sat in his truck shaking, unable to go inside, and realized his life was being run by efforts to avoid that moment. He says he wants his marriage and ordinary life back, but what he fears most is that the crash revealed a permanent truth—that the world is fundamentally dangerous, his body cannot be trusted, and the part of him that once felt alive may not return.
